title: Controllable Logical Hypothesis Generation
one_liner: When a doctor sees a symptom, there are hundreds of diseases that could explain it, but a good diagnosis needs the most plausible and relevant ones—this paper gives a way to steer hypothesis generation toward user-specified constraints.
lead: Abductive reasoning is the process of finding explanations for observations. Given a patient with a fever, you might infer they have the flu, a bacterial infection, or COVID-19—all are plausible. On large knowledge graphs, a single observation triggers thousands of possible hypotheses, most redundant or irrelevant. This paper adds a control knob so users can steer which hypotheses get generated, trading exploration for practical utility.

problem.h2: Too many plausible explanations, no control
paras: Knowledge graphs store facts as triples: doctor-diagnoses-patient, disease-causes-symptom. Given one entity (a patient with a fever), abductive reasoning asks: what diagnoses could explain this? The system finds all valid chains of reasoning—sometimes hundreds or thousands. A naive approach generates them all equally, flooding the user with irrelevant noise.

A doctor does not want all 200 possible diagnoses of a fever. They want the ones most likely for this specific patient, or ones matching a particular suspect (respiratory infection, not neurological). The system needs a way to accept user constraints—rules like prefer simpler explanations, or only show diagnoses of type X—and use those to filter the hypothesis space intelligently.

callout.html: Add a control setting that steers hypothesis generation toward user-specified constraints while keeping the hypotheses relevant and diverse.

steps.b: Start with a simple hypothesis model
steps.text: Train a baseline model to generate plausible chains of reasoning from an observation to candidate explanations.
Create training examples of shorter, simpler logical subpatterns—break complex hypotheses into pieces the model can reuse.
Teach the model to optimize multiple reward signals: match the user constraint, find semantically similar (relevant) hypotheses, and avoid repetition.
Reward 1 is how well the hypothesis matches the user's control condition. Reward 2 is how semantically similar it is to known good answers. Reward 3 gently penalizes redundancy.
Return hypotheses ranked by their total score: constrained and relevant, not just any plausible explanation.

object.h2: What the model learns to do differently
paras: The paper changes how the model generates the sequence of logical steps in a hypothesis. Instead of producing any valid chain, the model learns to assign higher probability to chains that satisfy a user constraint while remaining semantically relevant. The key change is not the architecture—it is the training objective, which now includes multiple reward signals pulling the hypothesis generation toward desirable behaviors.

hidden.name: How well the hypothesis matches the user constraint
paras: When a user specifies a control condition like 'only respiratory diseases' or 'prefer simpler chains,' the model needs to quantify how well a candidate hypothesis obeys it. This is the hidden quantity: a numerical score (between 0 and 1) that measures alignment. For a fever with control 'respiratory-only,' a hypothesis ending in 'pneumonia' scores high; one ending in 'heart arrhythmia' scores zero.

The paper computes this reward by checking whether the generated hypothesis's final entity or logical type matches the control specification. It also uses a semantic similarity score (Dice overlap or Jaccard similarity) to measure how much the reasoning chain overlaps with high-quality reference explanations. A smooth, blended reward combines both signals so the model gets clear feedback during training, because a sharp, binary constraint reward would make the model oscillate between satisfying the control and matching quality examples.

heat.caption: Darker means higher reward. Hypotheses matching the constraint and reference answers rank highest.

reads.html: A reward is a number that tells a learning algorithm which outputs are good. Here, the reward is high when a hypothesis matches what the user asked for and aligns with known correct answers.

The condition-adherence reward is computed as a weighted sum of constraint-satisfaction score and semantic similarity (Dice / Jaccard) to penalize redundancy and guide generation toward feasible, relevant hypotheses.

mechanism.h2: Why adding control rewards redirects hypothesis generation
paras: During training, the model learns by predicting the next logical step (entity or relation) and receiving a reward signal telling it whether the full chain was good. If unconstrained, the model learns to maximize any plausible explanation. But when the training adds a reward that specifically penalizes hypotheses violating the user constraint and boosts those matching it, the model's internal numbers representing 'good reasoning' shift, because the reinforcement learning algorithm repeatedly shows the model examples of chains it generated, their rewards, and nudges the model's weights toward higher-reward chains. Words, relations, and entity types associated with violating the constraint get lower scores in the model's hidden layers; those matching the constraint get higher scores. This is not filtering after the fact—it is retraining the model's internal decision-making.

A second challenge emerges: the model overfits to the control constraint and ignores semantic quality (relevance to known good answers). The paper solves this by smoothing the reward with multiple terms. Instead of a sharp constraint reward, the model balances: Does this match the control? Is this similar to ground-truth diagnoses? Have I already generated this before? The model learns to optimize all three together, trading off control-adherence against redundancy and semantic fidelity. The two-stage training (supervised learning, then reinforcement learning) helps, because the supervised stage primes the model with real examples of high-quality reasoning chains, so when reinforcement learning adds the constraint term, the model starts from a foundation that already values quality—it does not have to rediscover what good reasoning looks like.

stages.s: Model encodes the observation and constraint
Decode one step at a time, checking constraint
Score hypothesis on constraint + similarity + uniqueness
Update model weights to favor high-scoring chains

math.words: Total reward = Constraint-match score plus Semantic-similarity score minus Redundancy penalty
math.equation: R = w_c * S_c(h) + w_s * S_sim(h, ref) - w_r * penalty_redundant(h)
symbols: Constraint-satisfaction score (0 to 1; 1 if h matches user control)
Semantic similarity between hypothesis h and reference answers (Dice or Jaccard overlap)
Penalty if h is too similar to previously generated hypotheses
Weights controlling how much each term matters

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Hypothesis A: fever -> inflammation -> pneumonia. Constraint: respiratory. S_c(A) = 1.0. S_sim(A, gold refs) = 0.8. Penalty = 0. w_c=0.5, w_s=0.3, w_r=0.2. R = 0.5*1.0 + 0.3*0.8 - 0.2*0 = 0.5 + 0.24 = 0.74.
Hypothesis B: fever -> immune -> cardiac arrhythmia. Constraint: respiratory. S_c(B) = 0. S_sim(B, gold) = 0.1. Penalty = 0. R = 0.5*0 + 0.3*0.1 - 0.2*0 = 0.03.
Model learns to rank A (0.74) far above B (0.03). Reinforcement learning increases probability of chains like A.

math.note: The three terms represent adherence to the user's intent, alignment with known correct answers, and avoiding redundancy—the model trades off all three, weighted by w.

charts.title: Uncontrolled baseline
charts.note: Without control, the model spreads probability across all plausible hypotheses, many irrelevant.

items.html: If the user constraint is very specific (e.g., only three entities allowed), the model may learn to always generate the same three hypotheses. Semantic diversity collapses.
If the constraint-match reward and semantic-similarity reward pull in different directions (constraint wants X, gold data prefers Y), the model oscillates or gets stuck at a local compromise.
If the constraint weight is too high, the model ignores semantic quality and generates any chain satisfying the control. Tuning the three weights for each dataset requires experimentation.

The paper uses smoothed rewards (Dice and Jaccard overlap) and tests different weight values on held-out validation sets before final testing. Multiple reward terms prevent collapse into a single degenerate hypothesis.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small knowledge graph of animals and their properties (has-four-legs, is-mammal, eats-meat, lives-in-forest). Pick an observation like 'I see an animal that is fast.' Ask the system to generate hypotheses both unconstrained and constrained to 'predators only.' Measure: How many generated hypotheses end in a predator? How much do they overlap with a reference set of correct predator answers? How many times does the system repeat the same hypothesis? The demo should show that constrained generation has higher predator-matching rate, no loss of relevance, and much lower redundancy.
demo.metric_eq: Constraint adherence = count(hypotheses matching constraint) / total hypotheses. Semantic quality = average overlap with reference answers. Redundancy = count(duplicate hypotheses) / total.
demo.closing: The deepest finding: the same model, with the same architecture, produces radically different hypotheses if you add a reward term that explicitly values user constraints. This is steering, not filtering.
